c.tagline: Anguilla's low-key island capital, a gateway to barefoot-luxury resorts and some of the Caribbean's finest white-sand beaches.

taxi.fareNote: There are no ride-hailing apps on Anguilla. A fleet of licensed taxis uses government-set flat fares by zone (a dispatcher issues a fare slip at the airport and ferry terminal). Pay in cash or card, and note drivers also offer multi-hour island tours.

emergency.note: 911 reaches police, fire and ambulance island-wide. Anguilla's single hospital, Princess Alexandra Hospital, is in The Valley.

english.label: Easy to get by in English

avoid.reason: Petty theft is rare, but don't leave valuables on beaches or in unlocked cars.

hood_desc: The island's small commercial and administrative capital, home to Wallblake House (Anguilla's only surviving 1780s plantation home), St Gerard's Catholic Church, the Heritage Collection Museum and the government offices; the practical base near the airport, though most beaches are a short drive away.

A lively fishing-and-salt village on Road Bay whose beach is the heart of Anguilla's nightlife, with legendary beach bars and grills like Johnno's, Elvis' Beach Bar and The Pumphouse, plus boat trips to nearby Sandy Island; the best spot for sunset drinks and live local bands.

A mile-long stretch of powder-white sand and calm, reef-protected turquoise water often ranked among the world's best beaches; a cluster of low-key resorts, beach bars and snorkelling spots make it a relaxed, family-friendly base.

An upscale west-end beach lined with some of the island's most refined resorts and restaurants (Malliouhana, Blanchard's, Straw Hat); a fine strolling beach with a quiet, polished, barefoot-luxury feel.
A long, gently curving beach on the south coast with sweeping views across to St Martin, anchored by the CuisinArt/Aurora resort and a couple of laid-back beach bars; calm, spacious and relaxed.
lodging: Zemi Beach House, LXR Hotels & Resorts

water.note: Supply comes from desalination and cisterns; most visitors and locals drink bottled water.

transit.pay: Anguilla has no public bus or rail network. Licensed taxis charge government-set flat fares by zone, paid in cash or card; there is no transit card.
transit.hours: Taxis operate on demand day and night; arrange a return trip or take a driver's phone number in advance, especially after dark.
transit.note: There is no public transport on Anguilla. Getting around is by rental car or licensed taxi, and most visitors rent a car to reach the island's 30-plus beaches and scattered restaurants.

car.idp: A temporary Anguilla driving permit is required (issued on the spot for a small fee); most foreign licenses are accepted

ferry: Public ferry Blowing Point (Anguilla) - Marigot (French St Martin)
Fast-boat charters Blowing Point - Princess Juliana Airport (Sint Maarten / SXM)

transit.m: Taxi to Sandy Ground / west-end beaches (15-25 min)
Rental car (delivered to your hotel; no rental desks at the airport)

tip.r: Most hotels and restaurants add a 10-15% service charge; if it is not included, 10-15% is customary. A 10% government accommodation tax also applies.

food.desc: Local spiny lobster split, brushed with garlic butter and lime, and grilled over coals; the island's proudest catch, sold by the pound.

places.name: Palm Grove Bar & Grill

places.name: Tasty's Restaurant

food.name: Stewed Goat
food.desc: Anguilla's national dish: goat slow-braised with thyme, onion and peppers into a dark gravy, served over rice and peas.

places.name: Hungry's Good Food

places.name: Sarjai's Restaurant
places.note: Home-style Anguillian cooking; stewed goat and creole snapper are the standouts.

places.name: Tasty's Restaurant

food.name: Saltfish and Johnnycakes
food.desc: Fried or griddled cornmeal-and-flour cakes served with sauteed salt cod, onions and peppers; the classic Anguillian breakfast.

places.name: Tasty's Restaurant
places.note: Widely cited as the best place on island for saltfish with johnnycakes.

places.name: E's Oven

places.name: Palm Grove Bar & Grill
places.note: Johnnycakes and rice and peas served alongside the grill's seafood plates.

food.desc: Day-boat snapper scored, seasoned creole-style and grilled whole, usually with fungi, plantain and a squeeze of lime.

places.name: Sarjai's Restaurant

places.name: Roy's Bayside Grill

places.name: Palm Grove Bar & Grill

places.name: B&D's BBQ

places.name: Smokey's at the Cove
places.note: Beachfront shack pairing barbecue and ribs with live music and toes-in-sand seating.

food.name: Conch Stew and Conch Fritters
food.desc: Queen conch tenderised and simmered in creole gravy, or minced into peppery deep-fried fritters served with a lime dip.

places.name: Tasty's Restaurant
places.note: Conch appears in both stew and fritter form on this Anguillian institution's menu.

places.name: Hungry's Good Food
places.note: No-frills local spot where conch and other island staples rotate on the daily board.

places.name: Elvis' Beach Bar
places.note: Boat-shaped bar on the sand serving conch fritters with the sunset crowd.

food.name: Anguillian Rum Punch
food.desc: Caribbean rum shaken with lime, cane syrup, fruit juice and grated nutmeg; every beach bar guards its own ratio.

places.name: Elvis' Beach Bar
places.note: Iconic boat bar with a rum list of dozens of bottles and a famed house punch.

places.name: The Dune Preserve
places.note: Bankie Banx's driftwood beach bar, an Anguillian landmark for rum and live reggae.

places.name: Johnno's Beach Stop
places.note: Sunday-afternoon institution where rum punch comes with live island bands.

food.name: Mauby and Local Ginger Beer
food.desc: Non-alcoholic island staples: bittersweet mauby brewed from tree bark and spices, and fiery house-made ginger beer.

places.name: Hungry's Good Food
places.note: Local kitchen where house-brewed mauby and ginger drinks sit beside the lunch plates.

places.name: E's Oven

places.name: Ken's BBQ

landmarks: Wallblake House
Anguilla's oldest surviving plantation house, built in 1787 by sugar planters, offers a rare glimpse of colonial architecture with its restored kitchen and stables.
St. Gerard's Roman Catholic Church
An architectural curiosity beside Wallblake House, famed for its facade of embedded stones and open latticework walls that let sea breezes cool the congregation.
Anguilla Heritage Collection Museum
Historian Colville Petty's passionate collection of photographs, artefacts and documents traces island life from Arawak settlement through the 1967 Anguilla Revolution.
Old Valley Well and Historic Village
The stone well that once watered The Valley anchors a cluster of historic cottages and churches recalling Anguilla's quiet pre-tourism days.
Ebenezer Methodist Church
Anguilla's oldest church, dating from 1830, remains a dignified whitewashed landmark of island faith and a cornerstone of The Valley's historic quarter.
Fountain Cavern National Park
Anguilla's most important Amerindian site, a cave sanctuary near Shoal Bay containing a rare petroglyph of the deity Jocahu carved beside a freshwater pool.
Sandy Ground Village and Salt Pond
The island's boating and nightlife hub curves around a historic salt pond, where beach bars, fishing boats and sunset views define laid-back Anguillian life.
Crocus Bay and Little Bay
Dramatic cliffs shelter these calm snorkelling coves below Crocus Hill, the island's highest point; paddle round to secluded Little Bay for tropical-fish encounters.
Big Spring Heritage Site (Island Harbour)
A collapsed cave once used by Amerindians for ceremonies preserves dozens of ancient petroglyphs near the colourful fishing village of Island Harbour.
Crocus Hill
Anguilla's highest point at 65 metres, topped by the ruined Old Court House and offering a sweeping sunset view over the capital and its bays.

train.note: There is no railway on Anguilla. Arrive by air into Clayton J. Lloyd International Airport, served by small aircraft from St Maarten, Antigua and Puerto Rico, or by the frequent ferry from Saint-Martin.

bus.note: There is no public bus service on Anguilla. Taxis operate on fixed government rates and most visitors hire a car - the island is only 26 km long, and driving is on the left. There is no terminal.

intl.to: Marigot, Saint-Martin (France) - from Blowing Point, ~25 min
Sint Maarten - Princess Juliana airport (Netherlands) - from Blowing Point

ferry.note: The Marigot crossing is Anguilla's lifeline, running roughly every 45 minutes through the day from Blowing Point on the south coast, about 15 minutes from The Valley. It is a full international crossing with immigration at both ends, so carry your passport and expect a departure tax. Private charters run direct to St Maarten's airport, which is more convenient for connecting flights. Sailings are rough in winter swell.

half.name: Shoal Bay East
half.blurb: Regularly ranked among the world's best beaches, this two-mile ribbon of powder-white sand and luminous turquoise water lies minutes north of The Valley.
